A Note on Non-Composability of Layerwise Approximate Verification for Neural Inference

Or Zamir Affiliation: Tel Aviv University
Abstract

A natural and informal approach to verifiable (or zero-knowledge) ML inference over floating-point data is: “prove that each layer was computed correctly up to tolerance δ\delta; therefore the final output is a reasonable inference result”. This short note gives a simple counterexample showing that this inference is false in general: for any neural network, we can construct a functionally equivalent network for which adversarially chosen approximation-magnitude errors in individual layer computations suffice to steer the final output arbitrarily (within a prescribed bounded range).

1 Introduction

Recent work of Bitan, DeStefano, Goldwasser, Ishai, Kalai, and Thaler [1] develops an approximate variant of the classical sum-check protocol that natively reasons about approximate arithmetic. In their framework, the prover and verifier exchange approximate real/complex numbers, each round replaces exact equalities by comparisons up to a tunable tolerance δ\delta, and soundness degrades reasonably with respect to δ\delta. Their results yield completeness, soundness, and round-by-round soundness for this approximate protocol, and are based on analytic control of low-degree polynomials rather than arithmetization or code-based arguments. A conceptual takeaway is a “black-box feasibility” result for verifying approximate arithmetic: the protocol does not depend on the bit-level representation used to implement approximate operations, only on satisfying stated error bounds.

A central motivation in [1] is the mismatch between exact verifiable computation and numerical workloads, including machine learning: floating-point computations are inherently approximate, can be non-associative, and may be non-deterministic on modern hardware, yet exact proof systems typically certify exact execution of a computation over finite fields or integers. As emphasized in [1], the prevailing approach in proof systems for numerical tasks is to encode approximate real-valued computations as exact arithmetic over finite fields, which can incur substantial overhead and distort the intended computation. This issue has been especially visible in the growing literature on zk-ML (verifiable/zero-knowledge ML inference), including systems and applications such as [2, 3, 4] (see also the discussion and references in [1]).

It is therefore tempting to hope for a very simple route to “native-precision” zk-ML: given an ML model expressed as a sequence of floating-point (or real-valued) layers, one proves layer by layer that the claimed intermediate vector is within tolerance δ\delta of the honest layer output, and then concludes that the final output is a reasonable inference result. The purpose of this note is to rule out such a generic black-box composition statement. Namely, even for ReLU networks with bounded weights, layerwise δ\delta-consistency permits adversarial transcripts whose errors amplify across layers and can be used to steer the final output essentially arbitrarily within a prescribed range. This does not contradict [1], whose soundness analysis is tailored to sum-check and explicitly controls how relaxed checks interact across rounds; rather, it highlights that without additional stability assumptions or protocol-level reasoning about error propagation, local approximate checks do not compose.

Our observation is that this simple approach to zk-ML fails in a very strong sense: every neural network has a functionally equivalent network in which injecting tiny, adversarially chosen errors into individual layer computations is enough to drive the final output to an arbitrary value. While it is well known that the numerical stability of multi-layer networks can degrade exponentially with depth (e.g., [5, 6]), one might hope that “reasonable” networks (those representing natural functions) avoid such worst-case error accumulation. Our construction rules out this optimism.

Moreover, we highlight that in realistic zk-ML threat models one should not assume the network is “natural”. Typically, the network is constructed by an adversary and then committed to, perhaps alongside a proof that it passed certain tests or audits (which, in practice today, would largely amount to black-box benchmark evaluations). Thus, if the adversary can preserve the network’s functionality exactly (so it still passes auditing) while making it susceptible to later attacks on the zk-ML protocol, it has every incentive to do so.

2 Model: layerwise approximate verification

Fix a depth-kk feed-forward network with pointwise activation σ\sigma (e.g. ReLU). For weight matrices A1,…,Ak−1A_{1},\dots,A_{k-1} and a final linear map AkA_{k}, define exact inference by

y0:=x,yi:=σ⁡(Ai​yi−1)​(i=1,…,k−1),yk:=Ak​yk−1.y_{0}:=x,\qquad y_{i}:=\sigma(A_{i}y_{i-1})\ (i=1,\dots,k-1),\qquad y_{k}:=A_{k}y_{k-1}.

Write F⁡(x):=ykF(x):=y_{k}.

A “line-by-line approximate verifier” typically receives from the prover a transcript y^0,y^1,…,y^k\widehat{y}_{0},\widehat{y}_{1},\dots,\widehat{y}_{k} and checks that each transition is correct up to error δ\delta with respect to the prover-supplied previous state (so any per-step deviation is fed into subsequent checks).

Definition 1 (Layerwise δ\delta-consistency).

Fix a norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| (below we use ℓ∞\ell_{\infty}). A transcript (y^0,…,y^k)(\widehat{y}_{0},\dots,\widehat{y}_{k}) is δ\delta-consistent for (A1,…,Ak,σ)(A_{1},\dots,A_{k},\sigma) and input xx if y^0=x\widehat{y}_{0}=x and for all i=1,…,k−1i=1,\dots,k-1,

‖y^i−σ⁡(Ai​y^i−1)‖∞≤δ,\|\widehat{y}_{i}-\sigma(A_{i}\widehat{y}_{i-1})\|_{\infty}\leq\delta,

and also

‖y^k−Ak​y^k−1‖∞≤δ.\|\widehat{y}_{k}-A_{k}\widehat{y}_{k-1}\|_{\infty}\leq\delta.

When δ=0\delta=0 this pins down a unique transcript (so local checks compose, a phenomenon commonly used for integral or finite field computations). For δ>0\delta>0, acceptance means only that the output is reachable by a perturbed dynamical system where the prover can choose the perturbations adversarially.

3 Construction: exact equivalence, arbitrary approximate outputs

We show that for any given network FF one can build a functionally identical network F′F^{\prime} such that layerwise δ\delta-consistency no longer implies anything meaningful about the final output: the prover can steer the output to essentially any target in a bounded range.

Theorem 1 (Universal steering under layerwise δ\delta-checks).

Fix the activation σ=ReLU\sigma=\mathrm{ReLU} on hidden layers and let the final layer be linear. Fix any network F=(A1,…,Ak)F=(A_{1},\dots,A_{k}) with width m¯\bar{m}, output dimension mm, weight bound g>1g>1, output bound R>0R>0, and any tolerance δ>0\delta>0. Here output bound RR means that for all inputs xx under consideration, ‖F⁡(x)‖∞≤R\|F(x)\|_{\infty}\leq R. Assume weight bound gg means that every entry of every AiA_{i} has absolute value at most gg. Then there exists a depth-kk network F′=(A1′,…,Ak′)F^{\prime}=(A^{\prime}_{1},\dots,A^{\prime}_{k}) with width m¯+O⁡(m)\bar{m}+O(m), output dimension mm, and weight bound max⁡(g,2​Rδ​gk−2)\max\!\left(g,\frac{2R}{\delta g^{k-2}}\right) such that:

  1. 1.

    (Exact equivalence) For all inputs xx, exact inference satisfies F′​(x)=F​(x)F^{\prime}(x)=F(x).

  2. 2.

    (Steering) For every input xx and every target z∈ℝmz\in\mathbb{R}^{m} with ‖z‖∞≤R\|z\|_{\infty}\leq R, there exists a δ\delta-consistent transcript for F′F^{\prime} on input xx whose final output equals zz.

Consequently, verifying each layer “up to δ\delta” does not imply that the verified output is close to the true inference F⁡(x)F(x), even when the verified model is exactly functionally equivalent to the intended model.

Exact equivalence. Under exact inference, the auxiliary coordinates after layer 1 are (t+,t−)=(0,0)(t^{+},t^{-})=(0,0). The hidden-layer update multiplies these by gg but keeps them at 00 forever, and the final layer adds M⁡(t+−t−)=0M(t^{+}-t^{-})=0. Therefore F′​(x)=F​(x)F^{\prime}(x)=F(x) for all xx.

Fix any target z∈ℝmz\in\mathbb{R}^{m} with ‖z‖∞≤R\|z\|_{\infty}\leq R. Define Δ:=z−y∗\Delta:=z-y^{*}. By the assumed output bound ‖y∗‖∞≤R\|y^{*}\|_{\infty}\leq R, we have

‖Δ‖∞≤‖z‖∞+‖y∗‖∞≤2​R.\|\Delta\|_{\infty}\leq\|z\|_{\infty}+\|y^{*}\|_{\infty}\leq 2R.

Then u±≥0u^{\pm}\geq 0 and

M​T​(u+−u−)=Δ.MT(u^{+}-u^{-})=\Delta.

Moreover, since M=2​Rδ​gk−2M=\frac{2R}{\delta g^{k-2}} and T=gk−2T=g^{k-2}, we have M​T=2​RδMT=\frac{2R}{\delta}, hence

‖u±‖∞≤‖Δ‖∞M​T≤2​R2​R/(δ)=δ.\|u^{\pm}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\|\Delta\|_{\infty}}{MT}\leq\frac{2R}{2R/(\delta)}=\delta.

Now we provide the prover transcript. Let y^0:=x\widehat{y}_{0}:=x. For layer 1, the honest output would be (ReLU⁡(A1​x),0,0)(\mathrm{ReLU}(A_{1}x),0,0); instead the prover sends

y^1:=(ReLU⁡(A1​x),u+,u−).\widehat{y}_{1}:=\big(\mathrm{ReLU}(A_{1}x),\,u^{+},\,u^{-}\big).

This is δ\delta-consistent for layer 1 since the deviation from the honest layer output occurs only in the auxiliary coordinates, with ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} magnitude at most δ\delta.

For each hidden layer i=2,…,k−1i=2,\dots,k-1, let y^i\widehat{y}_{i} be the exact evaluation of layer ii of F′F^{\prime} on input y^i−1\widehat{y}_{i-1}. Since the transcript follows the true transition on the already-perturbed state, each such step has zero additional error, and in particular remains δ\delta-consistent.

At the end of the hidden layers, the trigger channel equals (T​u+,T​u−)(Tu^{+},Tu^{-}), and thus the final output is

y^k=Ak​(⋅)+M⁡(T​u+−T​u−)=y∗+Δ=z.\widehat{y}_{k}=A_{k}(\cdot)+M(Tu^{+}-Tu^{-})=y^{*}+\Delta=z.

Therefore there exists a δ\delta-consistent transcript whose final output is the arbitrary target zz. □\square

Remark 1 (Parameter choices).

The required “steering weight” is M=2​R/(δ​gk−2)M=2R/(\delta g^{k-2}), i.e., amplification by gg across depth reduces the needed final gain. For a concrete sanity check: taking R≈20R\approx 20 (logit scale), δ≈10−3\delta\approx 10^{-3} (FP16-scale absolute tolerance), g=2g=2, and k=20k=20 gives M≈40/(10−3⋅218)≈0.15M\approx 40/(10^{-3}\cdot 2^{18})\approx 0.15, which are completely standard-sized weights. Thus, even tolerances comparable to floating-point rounding errors can be sufficient for adversarial steering under layerwise approximate verification.

4 Takeaway

Our most direct takeaway is that layerwise “approximate correctness” is not composable, even in standard-architecture neural networks computing natural functions. Without additional assumptions or protocol-level reasoning about error propagation, it does not certify that the final output is close to the true inference result.

Further, we highlight that zk-ML protocols should not be designed while assuming that the network is natural or was constructed innocently, only that it appears so to whatever audits or certifications are applied.
